1.note: The print reads ha-peri, "the fruit". Sense taken: the miracle had no visible result and no public witnesses.

2.note: Taken as Jean Fernel (Fernelius) and his book on the method of healing. The identification and the chapter are not checked.

3.note: Probably the Margarita philosophica of Gregor Reisch, book 9, chapter 24. Not checked. The chapter number looks like פב"ד in the Vilna print; taken as פכ"ד (24).

4.he: כי אפילו של עצמות וגידין לא פעלו בו מאומה
4.note: The syntax is short. Sense taken: if the beak and claws did not peck, there was no need for metal ones.

5.note: The name is transliterated. The writer is not identified.

6.note: The Vilna print reads ה"ב; taken as ח"ב, "part 2". Guide 2:6 does speak against those who read the sages literally.

7.note: The square brackets are in the Vilna print: a correction by the editor.

8.note: The author's marginal note here names "Tully" (Cicero) and, it seems, his speech for Roscius. The first title in the note is not legible to the translator.

9.note: The print reads 68. In current editions the story is in Bereshit Rabbah 64.

10.note: The bird in the midrash is the "Egyptian kore", usually taken as a heron or crane. In Aesop the fable is the wolf and the crane.

11.he: הרופא הטוב בספרו השני מן הרעש
11.note: Taken as a play on the name of the physician Buoni, the author of a dialogue on the earthquake. "The good physician" is also possible.

12.note: Read as Seleucia. Trajan died at Selinus in Cilicia.

13.note: The Vilna print reads ושדך; taken as ושכך, "and calmed".
